title: The history of the mobile phone
tagline: Eighty years from phones bolted into cars to a billion Indian connections and a supercomputer in every pocket.
intro: Radio could carry voices long before anyone could carry the radio. The breakthrough was an idea from 1947: cut a city into small cells and reuse the same channels again and again. It took computers and chips to make it work. Then phones went digital, learned to text, joined the internet, and in India, cheap data in 2016 brought hundreds of millions of people online for the first time.

eras.name: Radio telephones
eras.summary: Phones in cars, one big transmitter per city, and the idea of cells on paper.

eras.name: The first mobiles
eras.summary: A handheld call in New York, then analogue 1G networks in Japan, the Nordic countries and the USA. Brick phones for the rich.

eras.name: Going digital
eras.summary: GSM turns voice into encrypted numbers and adds texting. Mobiles spread worldwide.

eras.name: India dials in
eras.summary: From a first call in Kolkata to a billion connections, cheap handsets and then the Jio data revolution.

eras.name: Phones become computers
eras.summary: Email, the mobile web, cameras, 3G, then touchscreens and app stores.

eras.name: Everything is data
eras.summary: 4G carries calls, video and payments as internet packets.

eras.name: 5G and after
eras.summary: Wider channels, beam-steering antennas and new bands, and the challenge of e-waste.

events.title: A secret way to hop between frequencies
events.text: Film star Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil patented a way to stop radio-guided torpedoes being jammed: the sender and receiver hop between frequencies in the same secret order. The navy shelved it at the time.
events.why: Frequency hopping and spread-spectrum ideas later helped make crowded digital radio, including some phone systems, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, work.

events.title: Phones in cars
events.text: The Mobile Telephone Service let drivers make calls from a heavy radio set in the boot. One big transmitter covered the whole city, so only a few calls could happen at once, and an operator connected every one.
events.why: It showed the demand, and the limit: one tower for a whole city could never serve many people.

events.title: The idea of cells
events.who: Douglas H. Ring and W. Rae Young, Bell Labs
events.text: In an internal memo, Bell Labs engineers proposed covering an area with many small low-power cells, each reusing the same channels as cells far enough away, and hexagons were used to draw them. The electronics to switch calls between cells did not exist yet.
events.why: Frequency reuse in small cells is still how every mobile network works.

events.title: The first handheld mobile call
events.text: Standing on Sixth Avenue, Motorola engineer Martin Cooper called Joel Engel, his rival at Bell Labs, on a prototype DynaTAC. It weighed about 1.1 kg and its battery gave some 30 minutes of talk after 10 hours of charging.
events.why: It proved a phone could belong to a person, not a car or a building.

events.title: The first cellular network
events.text: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone switched on the world's first automatic cellular network, for car phones in Tokyo. It was analogue 1G.
events.why: Many cells, automatic handover between them: the cellular idea finally worked at city scale.

events.title: NMT: phones that cross borders
events.text: The Nordic Mobile Telephone system opened in Sweden, then Norway, Denmark and Finland. It was the first network to let you roam across countries.
events.why: Countries agreeing one standard became the model for GSM.

events.title: AMPS and the brick phone
events.text: America's first commercial cellular network, AMPS, opened in Chicago. The Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, approved that September, went on sale for $3,995.
events.why: Mobile phones became something you could buy, if you were rich.

events.title: Why a text is 160 characters
events.text: Working on the GSM standard, Friedhelm Hillebrand typed out sentences and questions on a typewriter and counted: almost all fitted in 160 characters. That is exactly what fits in 140 bytes at 7 bits a letter.
events.why: The limit shaped texting, and later tweets.

events.title: The first GSM call
events.text: Finland's former prime minister Harri Holkeri made the first call on a GSM network, built by Nokia and Siemens for the operator Radiolinja. GSM was digital: voice became numbers, encrypted over the air.
events.why: GSM became the world's standard, and the one India adopted.

events.title: "Merry Christmas": the first text
events.text: Engineer Neil Papworth typed "Merry Christmas" on a computer and sent it to the phone of Vodafone director Richard Jarvis. Phones could not yet type texts back.
events.why: SMS grew into the most used data service in the world for twenty years.

events.title: A phone with a touchscreen
events.text: The IBM Simon Personal Communicator went on sale. It had a touchscreen, email, a calendar and apps, which is why it is often called the first smartphone. Its battery lasted about an hour.
events.why: It showed a phone could also be a pocket computer.

events.title: India's first mobile call
events.text: West Bengal's Chief Minister Jyoti Basu, at Writers' Building in Kolkata, called Union Telecom Minister Sukh Ram in Delhi on a Nokia handset, over the Modi Telstra network. Calls were costly, and for years even receiving one was charged.
events.why: It began the story of the world's second-largest mobile market.

events.title: BlackBerry and email in your pocket
events.text: RIM launched the BlackBerry 850, a two-way pager with a tiny keyboard that pushed email to you. Phone models followed from 2002 and became the favourite of business people and politicians.
events.why: Always-on email made the phone a work tool, and "CrackBerry" a word.

events.title: The mobile internet begins
events.text: DoCoMo's i-mode service put simple web pages, email and ringtone downloads on ordinary phones. Tens of millions of Japanese signed up within a few years.
events.why: It proved people would use the internet on a phone.

events.title: A camera in the phone
events.text: The Sharp J-SH04 was among the first phones sold with a built-in camera, 0.11 megapixels, and you could send the photo to another phone.
events.why: Today's phone cameras sell more cameras than every other kind put together (see CameraClear).

events.title: 3G goes live
events.text: DoCoMo launched FOMA, the first commercial 3G (WCDMA) network, promising up to 384 kbit/s for video calls and faster web.
events.why: Data, not voice, began to drive network design.

events.title: The phone for everyone
events.where: Worldwide, much of it made for India
events.text: The Nokia 1100, a tough, cheap phone with a torch and a dust-proof keypad, came out in 2003. It sold about 250 million units, among the best-selling electronic gadgets ever, many of them in India.
events.why: Cheap, rugged handsets brought mobile phones to villages and small towns.

events.title: The iPhone
events.text: Apple's iPhone, announced on 9 January and sold from 29 June, replaced the keypad with a large multi-touch screen and a full web browser. Its App Store followed in 2008.
events.why: It set the shape of the modern smartphone: one big screen, fingers, apps.

events.title: Android arrives
events.text: The HTC Dream (T-Mobile G1) was the first phone running Android. Because any maker could use it, Android spread to phones at every price.
events.why: Low-cost Android phones are what most people in India and the world use today.

events.title: 3G reaches India
events.text: State-owned MTNL started India's first 3G service in Delhi. Private operators followed after the 2010 spectrum auction.
events.why: Mobile internet in India began to be more than slow text pages.

events.title: 4G LTE switches on
events.text: TeliaSonera opened the first commercial LTE networks in Stockholm and Oslo, using OFDM and MIMO antennas. At first you needed a USB modem, not a phone.
events.why: LTE made the network carry everything, even voice, as internet packets.

events.title: India's first 4G
events.text: Airtel opened India's first 4G network in Kolkata, using TD-LTE. For years 4G stayed small, pricey and mostly in big cities.
events.why: India joined the 4G world, though the boom was still to come.

events.title: A billion mobile connections
events.text: TRAI's figures showed India's wireless subscriptions passing 1 billion (1.01 billion) by the end of 2015, with total phone connections having crossed 1 billion that May. Many people had more than one SIM.
events.why: India became the second country, after China, with a billion mobile connections.

events.title: Jio and the data revolution
events.text: Reliance Jio launched a 4G-only network with free voice calls and months of free data. Rivals slashed prices. According to TRAI, the average price of 1 GB fell from about ₹269 in 2014 to about ₹12 in 2018.
events.why: Hundreds of millions of Indians came online for the first time, on phones, and India became one of the world's biggest users of mobile data.

events.title: 5G arrives
events.who: SK Telecom, KT, LG U+ and Verizon
events.text: South Korea's three operators and America's Verizon switched on the first 5G phone networks within hours of each other. 5G adds wider channels, beam-steering antennas and millimetre-wave bands.
events.why: Faster, lower-delay links, and wireless broadband for homes.

events.title: 5G in India
events.who: Government of India, Jio and Airtel
events.text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched 5G at the India Mobile Congress. It spread unusually fast: Ookla found India's median mobile download speed rose from about 14 Mbit/s in September 2022 to about 50 Mbit/s in August 2023.
events.why: One of the fastest 5G rollouts anywhere, using the 3.5 GHz and 700 MHz bands.

events.title: 62 million tonnes of e-waste
events.text: The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 reported that the world threw away 62 million tonnes of electronics in 2022, and only 22.3% was properly collected and recycled.
events.why: Old phones hold gold, copper and cobalt: recycling them matters.

firsts.label: Mobile call in India
firsts.who: Jyoti Basu to Sukh Ram, Kolkata to Delhi

people.note: Chaired the GSM group that set the 160-character length of an SMS.

people.note: Made India's first mobile call, from Kolkata, on 31 July 1995.

series.title: India: average price of 1 GB of mobile data
series.caption: TRAI figures: the price of mobile data fell by more than 95% after 4G and Jio arrived.

points.label: April–June 2023: ₹9.44 revenue per GB (TRAI Performance Indicators)

series.title: India: wireless (mobile) subscriptions
series.caption: From ten million in 2002 to well over a billion: counted as SIM connections, and many people have two.

facts: A text message is 160 characters because that is what fits in 140 bytes at 7 bits a letter. In Hindi (Unicode) only 70 fit.
The first handheld mobile weighed about 1.1 kg and gave some 30 minutes of talk.
A 3.5 GHz radio photon carries about a millionth of the energy needed to knock an electron off an atom.
Your phone reports signal strength around −80 to −110 dBm: less than a millionth of a millionth of a watt.
In 2014 a gigabyte of mobile data in India cost about ₹269; by 2018 it was about ₹12.
